opus-5.5.text:
I'd be careful about speaking for Ken. He's the best person to explain his own decision, and I don't want to put words in his mouth or overstate any one person's influence.

What I can say is how I think about recruiting someone like Ken. A mathematician at that level has spent decades building intuition, taste, and a reputation, so leaving academia, even partly, is a big step. Usually it isn't one name that does it. It's whether the problem feels real and whether the people around it are serious.

For mathematicians, the worry about AI for math is often that it's hype: a model that gets lucky on competition problems but doesn't understand anything. So it matters a lot when the people involved are thoughtful about what reasoning and generalization actually mean, and honest about what current systems can't do. That kind of intellectual honesty is what a mathematician responds to. They want to know you're not going to claim you've solved math when you haven't.

The other piece is the mission itself. We're trying to build systems that can do verified mathematical reasoning, where every step can be formally checked, so the output isn't just plausible but provably correct. For someone who has spent a career on deep problems in number theory, the idea of a tool that could help explore conjectures and check arguments at scale, without sacrificing rigor, is exciting.

So if you ask me what persuades great mathematicians, it's credible people, a hard problem worth their time, and a commitment to rigor. I'd rather Ken tell you which of those mattered most to him.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it mattered because Ken is, first and foremost, a mathematician, and mathematicians are rightly skeptical of AI hype. If I had walked in alone and said "we're building an AI that does math," he would have been polite, but he would have heard that pitch many times before. François brought a different kind of credibility. He created Keras, he wrote the book on deep learning that a lot of people learned from, and he's also been one of the most honest critics of the field. He's the person who built the ARC benchmark precisely to show what current models can't do. So when someone like that says, "I believe this particular approach could actually get us to genuine reasoning," it carries weight that marketing never could.

And I think there was a second thing. Ken cares deeply about the next generation of mathematicians and about whether these tools will be real collaborators or just pattern matchers that produce plausible-looking nonsense. François shares that concern. Their conversations weren't about model sizes or benchmarks. They were about what it would mean for a system to actually understand a proof, to generalize to a new problem rather than retrieve something it had seen. That's a conversation Ken wanted to be part of. So François didn't persuade him in the sense of selling him. He signaled that this was a place where serious people were asking the right questions, and that was enough for Ken to want to come and ask them with us.

r002.rationale: It says Ken and François shared concerns about AI as a genuine mathematical collaborator and had conversations about proof understanding and generalization, which helped signal to Ken that the team was asking serious questions and made him want to join.

Having François involved helped signal that this could be that kind of collaboration. I wouldn’t want to speak for Ken, but I think that was part of the appeal.
